Legal support if you’re behind on mortgage payments.

Last updated: September 19, 2026

What a Foreclosure Attorney in Iowa
Can Do for You

For many homeowners facing financial difficulties, foreclosure can soon be a reality. But what does it mean when a lender forecloses, and how can a foreclosure lawyer in Iowa help you protect your home? At Henkels & Baker, PC, based in Dubuque, Iowa, we help homeowners understand their rights and what they can do before time runs out.

Iowa has a consistently high number of foreclosures. In the third quarter of 2023, it ranked 15th in the United States for foreclosure filings. A foreclosure lawyer plays a crucial role in guiding clients through Iowa’s legal process—explaining their rights, negotiating with lenders, and helping explore options to avoid losing their property.

Iowa uses a judicial foreclosure process. That means a lender has to go to court to take your home. That takes time. It also means you have chances to respond, catch up on payments, or explore other paths before a sale ever happens.

Many homeowners don’t realize how much control they still have. Iowa law provides real protections, including deadlines the lender should follow and options that remain open at different points in the process. A foreclosure lawyer in Iowa can help you see the full picture, not just the pressure in front of you.

How Henkels & Baker Helps Iowa Homeowners Fight Back

At Henkels & Baker, PC, our first step is a close review of your loan, your missed payments, and the notices you have received. We look at where you stand in the process right now. That tells us which options are still open to you.

Every homeowner’s situation is different. Some clients want to keep their home. Others need a path out of debt without losing everything else. We listen first, then build a plan around your goals — not a one-size-fits-all script.

One of the most common solutions we pursue is Chapter 13 debt relief. This option can pause a foreclosure the moment it is filed. It gives you time to catch up on missed payments through a structured plan. You keep your home while you work toward a fresh start. Our team handles the filing, the court, and the lender.

For some clients, Chapter 7 is a better fit. It may not save the home in every case, but it can wipe out other debts. That frees up money to focus on what matters most.

We also examine whether the lender complied with Iowa’s rules. Lenders are obligated to meet strict notice and filing requirements. If they missed a step, that matters.

A foreclosure lawyer Iowa homeowners work with should do more than file paperwork. We dig into the details of your case. We contact lenders directly when needed. We work toward loan modifications, payment plans, or other routes that may keep you in your home longer, or protect you from a deficiency judgment after a sale.

If you are also dealing with wage garnishment or other debt pressure, those issues connect. Solving one piece without looking at the full picture can leave you stuck. We take a broad view of your finances so the plan we build actually holds.

Understanding Foreclosure in Iowa

Iowa foreclosures follow strict legal procedures and specific timelines. Both the type of foreclosure used and the timing of notices heavily impact how the process unfolds.

Judicial vs. Nonjudicial Foreclosure in Iowa

Foreclosure in Iowa can proceed through judicial or nonjudicial means.

Judicial foreclosure involves a court process. If the borrower doesn’t cure the default after receiving notice, the lender may file a lawsuit, and the property can be sold at auction if the lender prevails.

Nonjudicial foreclosure is less common and only allowed in limited cases (e.g., non-agricultural, non-owner-occupied properties). It requires a borrower-lender agreement, with the borrower voluntarily giving up the property and redemption rights.

Timeline and Notice Requirements

Lenders need to wait 120 days after delinquency before starting foreclosure. Borrowers then receive a 30-day notice of default, which details the amount owed and the deadline to cure the default. Paying the overdue amount during this period can stop the foreclosure process.

Foreclosure Sale and Redemption Period

If the default isn’t cured, the property may be sold at a public auction. Borrowers typically have a redemption period—a limited time to reclaim the property by paying the full amount owed.

Why Henkels & Baker Stands Apart for Iowa Homeowners

Henkels & Baker, PC brings a focused, client-first approach to foreclosure defense in Iowa. Each differentiator below is grounded in what our firm actually does.

Full-Service Debt Relief Practice Centered in Dubuque

Foreclosure does not happen in a vacuum. It usually comes with other debt pressures — missed bills, wage garnishment, or credit card balances. Our firm handles Chapter 7 and Chapter 13 debt relief, as well as foreclosure defense. That means we look at your entire financial picture, not just one piece.

Your Property Is Our Priority

We work diligently to pursue every available option to help clients retain property they want to keep. This is not a marketing claim. We work diligently to identify available options — catching up on payments, restructuring debt, or halting a sale — before anything is lost.

Free Consultations — No Pressure, No Guessing

You should know where you stand before you commit to anything. Our firm offers free consultations so you can ask real questions and get real answers. We serve a wide area around Dubuque, including parts of Illinois. You do not need to live downtown to get our help.

Serving Iowa Since 2018

Our firm has been helping clients in the Dubuque area since 2018. We focus on debt relief and related legal matters — not a broad mix of unrelated cases. That focus means we know the local courts, the Iowa foreclosure process, and the debt relief tools that can help you move forward.

What Happens During an Iowa Foreclosure Case

In Iowa, foreclosure is primarily judicial, meaning the process goes through the court system. Lenders need to file a lawsuit when a homeowner defaults on their mortgage. This usually applies to residential properties up to two-family dwellings.

During the litigation process, homeowners have options like filing bankruptcy to delay the sale or making the loan current under certain circumstances.

The typical judicial foreclosure process involves several key steps: 

Stage 1: Default and the Right to Cure (Days 1–30)

You miss payments. Your lender marks the loan in default. Before filing in court, Iowa law requires the lender to send a notice of right to cure.

You have 30 days to catch up on missed payments and stop the process. At this stage, Henkels & Baker, PC reviews your mortgage terms and helps you determine whether catching up is realistic or if another path makes more sense.

Stage 2: Court Filing and Service (Weeks 4–8)

If you do not cure the default, the lender files a petition in your county’s district court. Iowa Code Chapter 654 governs this step. You will be served with the lawsuit. You have 20 days to respond if served in person. You have 60 days if served by publication. Borrowers can negotiate, reinstate the loan, or pursue other legal options. If unresolved, the case proceeds to trial.

Our team helps you file a timely answer and flags any errors the lender made.

Stage 3: The Court Process (Months 2–6)

The case moves through the Iowa district court system. The lender is required to prove their claim. You have the chance to raise defenses.

This stage can last weeks or months, depending on the court’s schedule and what issues arise. An Iowa debt relief option like Chapter 13 may also come into play here — filing can pause the foreclosure under federal law.

Stage 4: Judgment and Sale (Months 4–8)

If judgment favors the lender, the property is sold at a public auction. Iowa law sets rules on how the sale is advertised and run.

Foreclosure auctions in Iowa are conducted by the local County Sheriff’s Offices and typically take place in person at the County Courthouse (e.g., at the front door, west entrance, or inside the lobby), a designated Sheriff’s office, or a local Law Enforcement Center.

At this point, your options narrow, but they do not disappear. A Chapter 7 or Chapter 13 filing before the sale date may still halt the process.

Stage 5: Redemption Period (Up to 12 Months Post-Sale)

After foreclosure, Iowa homeowners may redeem the property by paying the full debt within the statutory redemption period. This period is typically one year, but it can be shortened to six months, three months, or sixty days, depending on the situation (e.g., lender waives deficiency judgment or property is abandoned). They can also file a Demand for Delay of Sale for more time.  

If the sale doesn’t cover the loan balance, the lender may seek the remaining amount through a court order. Iowa courts can limit this based on fair market value — but you need to be ready for that fight.

Henkels & Baker, PC, provides experienced legal support to help homeowners navigate each step of the foreclosure process.

Know Your Legal Rights During Foreclosure

Right to Cure

Iowa law gives homeowners 30 days to cure the default after receiving a cure notice—by catching up on missed payments to stop foreclosure. Lenders are only required to provide one cure notice per 12-month period, so repeated defaults may not trigger additional notices.

Defending Against Foreclosure

Lenders are required to follow strict legal procedures before initiating foreclosure, including providing proper notice and documentation. Homeowners have the right to contest foreclosure in court, raising defenses such as improper paperwork, procedural violations, or predatory lending. If valid defenses are raised, the case may move into discovery, creating opportunities for settlement or negotiation.

items.q: What Steps Lenders Need to Take Before Starting Foreclosure In Iowa?
items.a: Foreclosure in Iowa generally begins with a judicial process. Before filing, the lender has to provide a “right to cure” notice—typically giving homeowners at least 30 days (or 45 days for agricultural properties) to catch up on missed payments and fees. Only if the default persists can the lender proceed by filing a formal foreclosure petition in court.

items.q: What Happens Once A Foreclosure Lawsuit Is Filed?
items.a: After the foreclosure complaint is filed, a summons and petition are served to the homeowner. Homeowners have 20 days to respond. If they do not contest the lawsuit, the lender may seek a default judgment, allowing the court to authorize a property sale without further delay. If contested, the matter may go through the court process, potentially involving summary judgment or trial.

items.q: How Is A Foreclosure Sale Conducted In Iowa?
items.a: Upon judgment, the property is then scheduled for a public auction, usually handled by the county sheriff. Notices should be posted in three public locations (including the courthouse) and published in local newspapers—starting at least four weeks before the sale. If the homeowner occupies the property, they also need to be personally served with notice at least 20 days in advance. Auctions typically occur during business hours, and the highest bidder—potentially the lender—wins the property.

items.q: Can Homeowners Still Reclaim Their Property After A Foreclosure Sale?
items.a: Yes. Iowa offers a right of redemption, allowing homeowners to reclaim the foreclosed property by paying the full amount owed—including fees and expenses—within a set period after the sale. The standard redemption period is one year, though it may be shortened to six months (or even 60 days) depending on conditions such as a waived deficiency judgment or property type.

items.q: What Legal Protection Or Alternatives Exist For Homeowners Facing Foreclosure?
items.a:
Homeowners can:

  • Reinstates their mortgage by paying arrears before the foreclosure process advances;
  • Explore alternatives like loan modifications, mediation, short sales, or deeds in lieu of foreclosure;
  • File for bankruptcy, which triggers an automatic stay that halts foreclosure proceedings temporarily;
  • Seek qualified legal counsel to evaluate options and help defend their rights at any stage of the process.
